name: HMB
lead: HMB (beta-hydroxy-beta-methylbutyrate) is a metabolite of the essential amino acid leucine that the body produces naturally; roughly 5 percent of dietary leucine is converted to it [4][3]. Two supplement forms have been studied, a calcium salt (HMB-Ca) and a free acid (HMB-FA) [1].

It is marketed to lifters and athletes for reducing muscle damage and muscle protein breakdown and for supporting recovery, and it is also used in clinical oral nutritional supplements for older and ill patients [1][5][6]. The chain people describe runs from less muscle breakdown and faster recovery, to more or harder training, to more muscle and a leaner physique over time; supporters also use it while dieting in the hope of holding on to lean mass [13][14].

The research picture differs by population. The International Society of Sports Nutrition (ISSN) position stand states that HMB's proposed mode of action is a dual effect, enhancing muscle protein synthesis and suppressing breakdown, and that chronic intake appears safe for up to at least a year [1]. A 2018 meta-analysis of six trials in trained athletes reported no significant effects on strength or body composition, whereas results in older adults and in clinical conditions are more often positive but vary by study [2][7].

chain: Leucine metabolite taken as a supplement
Proposed to raise muscle protein synthesis and lower breakdown
Less muscle damage and faster recovery between sessions
More training or retained lean mass, supporting physique
angle.text: Lifters take HMB hoping to limit muscle damage and recover faster, which they link to more productive training and better lean mass. The appearance payoff is a more muscular physique over time; studies report the clearest effects in untrained and older people.

paras: HMB is taken by resistance trainers and endurance athletes, especially during periods of heavy training volume, to try to limit muscle damage. T Nation members describe adding HMB to stacks to cope with training volume or recover faster [12][13][14]. It also appears in stacks of users who combine it with other supplements and, in some posts, with prescribed hormonal therapies [15].
HMB is an ingredient in specialized oral nutritional supplements studied in malnourished older adults, sarcopenia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, cancer and bed rest [5][6][8][9][10][11].

Two supplement forms are on the market: the calcium salt (HMB-Ca), sold as capsules or powder, and the free acid (HMB-FA), a gel or liquid form.[1] Wikipedia describes the usual supplemental intake as a multiple of the few tenths of a gram a healthy adult makes each day, and reports that muscle-damage reduction in studies appeared greatest when HMB-Ca was taken one to two hours before exercise or HMB-FA 30 to 60 minutes before.[3] Product makers sometimes pair HMB with creatine, and Wikipedia reports evidence that creatine may add to HMB's effects on performance and body composition; a crossover trial of creatine plus HMB in physically active older adults examined functional strength.[3][10]

In medical nutrition HMB appears in Abbott's Juven, which combines HMB-Ca with arginine and glutamine, and in Revigor and some Ensure formulations; Wikipedia reports Juven improved lean body mass in trials in people with AIDS and cancer but not in rheumatoid cachexia.[3]

The ISSN 2025 position stand summarises the field in twelve points. It concludes that HMB may reduce muscle damage and aid recovery and repair; that, combined with exercise, it may increase lean mass, reduce fat mass or both, with benefits most pronounced under demanding resistance training and dietary control; that it may improve strength and power in untrained people while results in trained athletes are mixed and tend to improve in studies longer than six weeks; and that it may benefit muscle strength, function and quality in sedentary and older adults and counter disuse atrophy.[1]

A 2018 meta-analysis of six randomised trials with 193 trained and competitive athletes found no significant effect on strength or body composition: effect sizes were 0.00 for bench press, 0.09 for leg press, 0.16 for fat-free mass and -0.20 for fat mass, with no heterogeneity across studies.[2] A 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis of seven trials with 287 older adults found greater muscle mass gain with HMB (standardised mean difference 0.352 kg, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.594) and no significant difference in fat mass, and its authors called for more research on strength and function.[7] Wikipedia's summary likewise describes evidence in trained athletes as mixed and larger effects in untrained people and those training intensely.[3]
A review of HMB in healthy and muscle-wasting conditions in 2017 discussed results across populations [16]. A 2022 systematic review examined HMB in patients with cancer [17].

Trials that combined HMB with other nutrients include a trial of a specialized oral nutritional supplement with dietary counselling in community-dwelling older adults at risk of malnutrition [5] and a multicentre trial of a high-protein HMB supplement on readmission and mortality in hospitalised malnourished older adults [6]. Because these are multi-ingredient products, the contribution of HMB cannot be separated.

The ISSN position stand states that available safety and toxicity data suggest chronic HMB-Ca and HMB-FA use is safe for up to at least one year and that HMB does not negatively affect glucose tolerance or insulin sensitivity [1].

Wikipedia reports that no adverse effects were found in young or older adults taking HMB for up to a year, or in young adults at twice the usual intake for two months, and that data in people under 18 are limited.[3] No clinical testing has been done in pregnant women, and the licensing company advises pregnant and lactating women not to take it.[3]

The primary mechanism proposed is a combined stimulation of muscle protein synthesis and suppression of protein breakdown, and the ISSN notes that HMB activates mTORC1 independently of the leucine-sensing Sestrin2-GATOR2 pathway [1]. Wikipedia adds that reduced breakdown may involve inhibition of the proteasome, that the full human mechanism is not identified, and that animal studies suggest roles for growth hormone, IGF-1 and cholesterol synthesis supporting muscle cell membranes.[3] A 2013 study compared the effects of leucine and HMB on human skeletal muscle protein metabolism [18].

Wikipedia describes the downstream chemistry: HMB is converted to HMB-CoA and feeds into HMG-CoA, which can go to acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate or into the mevalonate pathway toward cholesterol, and animal studies suggest HMB-derived cholesterol may support muscle cell membrane integrity.[3] It also reports that HMB is believed to activate mTOR signalling via p70S6 kinase and 4EBP1.[3]

HMB is produced when leucine is converted to alpha-ketoisocaproate and then partly to HMB; most dietary leucine follows other metabolic routes [4]. A healthy adult makes a few tenths of a gram per day, and foods contain only negligible amounts, so supplements supply far more than diet.[3] The ISSN statement reports that HMB-FA appears to raise blood HMB more than HMB-Ca, though recent results are mixed [1]; Wikipedia gives half-lives of about 2.5 hours for HMB-Ca and 3 hours for HMB-FA, with roughly 10 to 40 percent of a dose excreted unchanged in urine.[3]

Roughly 95 percent of leucine is metabolised mainly toward isovaleryl-CoA, and about 5 percent (range 2 to 10 percent) becomes HMB, mostly through alpha-ketoisocaproate and the liver enzyme KIC dioxygenase.[3]

Wikipedia traces HMB to its first synthesis in 1877 by Russian chemists Michael and Alexander Zaytsev, isolation from the bark of the Madagascan tree Erythrophleum couminga by Leopold Ruzicka in 1941, and identification as a human metabolite by Tanaka and colleagues in 1968, from a patient with isovaleric acidemia.[3]

Steven Nissen at Iowa State University described its effects on human skeletal muscle in the mid-1990s. He later founded Metabolic Technologies, Inc. (MTI), which holds HMB-related patents and licenses HMB to supplement makers.[3] It reached the market in the late 1990s, first sold to athletes and bodybuilders, and Abbott Nutrition later acquired market rights to MTI's Juven (2003) and Revigor (2008) products.[3]

Wikipedia reports that in 2006 about 2 percent of US college student athletes said they used HMB, and that use among young athletes was described as widespread by 2017.[3] The 2025 ISSN position stand is the most recent consolidated professional statement on the supplement.[1]

HMB was marketed in the late 1990s and early 2000s in bodybuilding magazines and by supplement companies. T Nation threads from that period include members asking whether HMB was 'as good as Deca' and recalling saving money to buy 'super-advanced' HMB products alongside brands such as Myoplex, and one member described it as the start of a downfall for a prominent supplement figure, in the poster's view [19][20][21]. A later poster recalled an HMB study in which subjects were said to gain more than from steroids [22]. Forum members' present-day views range from adding HMB to regimens to saying most supplements add little beyond training, sleep and nutrition [23][12].

In the US it is sold as an over-the-counter dietary supplement and is unscheduled by the UN; as of 2018 the NCAA, WADA and other major sports bodies had not banned it, and the licensing company advises pregnant and lactating women not to take it because safety studies are lacking.[3] It is also an ingredient in some medical nutrition products such as Abbott's Juven and certain Ensure formulations.[3]

Meta-analyses: a 2018 analysis of six trials in 193 trained athletes found no significant effect on strength or body composition,[2] and a 2015 analysis of seven trials in 287 older adults found greater muscle mass gain.[7] The ISSN issued a position stand in 2025.[1]

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled bed rest trial enrolled 24 healthy older adults for 10 days of complete bed rest followed by 8 weeks of resistance rehabilitation, with HMB started before bed rest. Among the 19 evaluable participants, controls lost about 2.05 kg of lean mass while the HMB group's change was about -0.17 kg, a significant between-group difference; function measures did not differ, which the authors attributed to the small sample.[8]

Other randomised trials include a sarcopenia trial of HMB supplementation in older adults [9], a crossover trial of creatine plus HMB on functional strength independent of muscle mass in physically active older adults [10], and a trial of omega-3 with and without HMB in COPD [11]. A 2022 systematic review considered cancer patients [17].

Registered trials include HMB in resistance-trained men (NCT01508338, 44 participants), in older women (NCT02118181, 80), lung transplant candidates in rehabilitation (NCT07660991), hemodialysis patients (NCT01837238), ACL surgery recovery (NCT02602561), Crohn's disease with sarcopenia (NCT07171593), and cerebral palsy (NCT05384951) [25][26][27][28][29][30][31].

lore.intro: HMB has been discussed on T Nation since the early 2000s, first as a heavily marketed muscle supplement and later as a minor add-on to training stacks [19][20][21][14].

claims.believers: Early-2000s forum posts reference the claim that HMB was 'as good as Deca' and a study said to show better results than steroids [20][22]; a 2003 poster described HMB's reputation as a disappointment, comparing it to Deca claims [21].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand describes benefits as helping reduce muscle damage and promote recovery, not steroid-like effects [1]; a meta-analysis in trained athletes assessed strength and body composition [2].

claims.claim: HMB helps you recover faster and handle more training volume
claims.believers: A T Nation log writer reports that an HMB product helped handle volume and recover between workouts [12].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand says HMB may help reduce muscle damage and promote recovery [1].

claims.claim: HMB preserves muscle during illness, bed rest or ageing
claims.believers: Some members see HMB as a hedge against muscle loss during hard training or dieting [13][14].
claims.experts: A meta-analysis in older adults and trials of oral nutritional supplements containing HMB in older, malnourished and bed-rested people examined this question [5][6][7][8].

claims.claim: HMB is a safe, low-risk supplement
claims.believers: Users include it routinely among other supplements [14][15].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand reports chronic use appears safe for up to at least a year and without effects on glucose tolerance [1].

claims.claim: HMB works better stacked with creatine
claims.believers: Supplement stackers on forums add HMB alongside creatine and other products to get more from training.[13][14]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports evidence that creatine may enhance HMB's effects on performance and body composition, and a crossover trial in physically active older adults tested creatine plus HMB on functional strength.[3][10]

claims.believers: Lifters who use HMB describe taking it around training sessions to limit muscle damage.[12]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports muscle-damage reduction was greatest when HMB-Ca was taken one to two hours, or HMB-FA 30 to 60 minutes, before exercise.[3]
